related_questions.question: What is the life expectancy of someone who has an AVM?
related_questions.snippet: Prognosis and Life Expectancy If an AVM does rupture, the survival rate is about 90%. The morbidity rate is about another 25% and includes patients who survive but then have some kind of brain damage or neurologic deficit. All statistics considered, the risk of dying annually if you have an AVM is relatively low.

related_questions.question: What is the cause of AVM?

text_blocks.snippet: The exact cause of arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) is unknown, but they are generally believed to be congenital, meaning they are present at birth. Most AVMs develop during fetal development, though they may not be diagnosed until later in life. While most AVMs are not hereditary, there are rare cases where they may run in families or be associated with other inherited conditions.
snippet_highlighted_words: The exact cause of arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) is unknown, but they are generally believed to be congenital, meaning they are present at birth

list.title: Congenital:
list.snippet: AVMs are typically thought to arise during the early stages of fetal development when blood vessels form incorrectly.

list.title: Not typically hereditary:
list.snippet: While most AVMs are not passed down through families, some individuals may have a genetic predisposition or be affected by inherited conditions that increase the risk.

list.title: Possible genetic link:
list.snippet: Some AVMs may be associated with genetic mutations, but the exact genetic mechanisms are still under investigation.

list.title: Rarely acquired:
list.snippet: Although AVMs are typically congenital, in rare cases, they may develop later in life, possibly after head trauma, according to OHSU.

list.title: Location matters:
list.snippet: AVMs can occur in various parts of the body, but those located in the brain or spinal cord (cerebral AVMs) are more likely to cause significant symptoms and complications.

related_questions.question: How serious is an AVM?
related_questions.snippet: Because the tangled blood vessels in an AVM do not form properly, they can weaken and burst. If an AVM in the brain bursts, it can cause bleeding in the brain, which can lead to a stroke or brain damage. Bleeding in the brain is known as a hemorrhage. related_questions.question: What to avoid if you have an AVM?
related_questions.snippet: If possible, a person with an AVM should avoid any activities that may excessively elevate blood pressure, such as heavy lifting or straining, and they should avoid blood thinners like warfarin. A person with an AVM should have regular checkups with his or her doctor.

text_blocks.snippet: An arteriovenous malformation (AVM) is a rare medical condition where arteries and veins are abnormally connected, bypassing the normal capillary network. This abnormal connection can lead to various health problems due to disrupted blood flow and potential rupture.
snippet_highlighted_words: a rare medical condition where arteries and veins are abnormally connected, bypassing the normal capillary network

list.title: Abnormal Connection:
list.snippet: In an AVM, arteries, which carry blood away from the heart at high pressure, connect directly to veins, which carry blood back to the heart at low pressure, without the usual network of capillaries.

list.title: Bypass of Capillaries:
list.snippet: Capillaries are small blood vessels that allow for the exchange of oxygen and nutrients between blood and surrounding tissues. AVMs bypass this crucial step.

list.title: Location:
list.snippet: While AVMs can occur in various parts of the body, they are most commonly found in the brain and spinal cord.
Congenital: Most AVMs are believed to be congenital, meaning they are present at birth, though they may not cause symptoms until later in life.
Unknown Cause: The exact cause of AVMs is unknown, but it is not typically inherited.
Potential Genetic Factors: Some genetic conditions are associated with an increased risk of AVMs, such as Cobb syndrome, hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT), and Parkes Weber syndrome.

list.title: Variable:
list.snippet: Symptoms of AVMs can vary greatly depending on their location, size, and whether they have ruptured.

list.title: Asymptomatic:
list.snippet: Many people with AVMs experience no symptoms, especially during childhood.

list.title: Rupture:
list.snippet: A ruptured AVM can cause a sudden, severe headache, seizures, and other neurological symptoms similar to a stroke.

list.title: Common Symptoms:
list.snippet: Other common symptoms include headaches, seizures, weakness, numbness, vision problems, speech difficulties, and problems with movement or balance.
Bleeding: The most serious complication of an AVM is bleeding (hemorrhage), which can lead to stroke-like symptoms and even death.
Seizures: Seizures are another common complication, especially in brain AVMs.
Neurological Damage: If an AVM compresses surrounding brain or spinal cord tissue or disrupts blood flow, it can cause permanent neurological damage.
Imaging Tests: Doctors use imaging tests such as MRI, MRA, CT angiography, and cerebral angiography to diagnose AVMs.
Physical Exam: A physical exam and review of symptoms are also important for diagnosis.
Bruit: A bruit, a whooshing sound caused by turbulent blood flow through the AVM, may be heard with a stethoscope.
Observation: Some small, asymptomatic AVMs may be monitored with regular imaging.
Surgery: Open brain surgery may be used to remove the AVM, but it carries risks.
Endovascular Embolization: This minimally invasive procedure involves threading a catheter through blood vessels to the AVM and blocking it with a glue-like substance.
Gamma Knife Radiosurgery: This procedure uses focused radiation to treat the AVM.
Combination Therapy: Treatment may involve a combination of these approaches.
